title: Complementary angles: why 30 and 60 degrees share a range
idealItem: What it is: a robot scientist (understands the material it shares)
chapter: Meeting 3: Understanding the results and observations (parts 2 and 3)
asked: The notes say complementary angles give the same range. Why is that, and what's actually different between, say, thirty and sixty degrees? || If I want it to get there fastest, which one do I pick?
answer: Same range because R is proportional to sine two theta, and theta and ninety minus theta give the same sine two theta. What's different is time in the air and the peak height. Sixty degrees goes higher and stays up longer; thirty degrees is flatter and lands sooner, but they cover the same horizontal distance ideally. Pick thirty degrees. It has the shorter flight time for the same range.
why: It omits the quantitative comparisons: the 60° peak is 3 times higher and its flight time is √3 times longer.
